title: Generics and Generic Programming
description: How Python achieves generic-like flexibility dynamically, how Java's generics work, and C's generic programming techniques.
objectives: Understand Python's dynamic-typing approach to 'generic' code
Understand C's techniques for generic programming without language-level generics

content.heading: Python
content.body: Python needs no explicit generics mechanism, because its dynamic typing already makes ordinary code inherently 'generic' — a function like def first(items): return items[0] works with a list, a tuple, or any other indexable sequence, with no type parameter declared anywhere. Optional type hints (List[T] via typing, or the newer list[T] syntax) can express intended generic constraints for static analysis tools, but nothing is enforced by the language at runtime.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Generics (class Box<T> { ... }) are a genuine, compile-time-checked language feature: a parameterized type ensures, at compile time, that a Box<String> only ever holds Strings — this catches type errors before runtime and eliminates the need for unsafe casts that pre-generics Java code required. Generic type information is erased at runtime (type erasure), a deliberate implementation choice for backward compatibility, meaning generics exist purely as a compile-time safety mechanism.

content.heading: C
content.body: C has no generics as a language feature at all. Generic-like behavior is achieved through other techniques: void* (a generic, type-less pointer) combined with an explicit size parameter, as qsort() in the standard library does; function-like macros, which are expanded textually and so work with any type the expansion happens to be valid for, at the cost of no type checking whatsoever; or, in more modern C (C11+), _Generic, a compile-time mechanism to select different code based on an expression's type. None of these provide anything close to Java's compile-time-checked type parameters.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python achieves generic-like flexibility simply by virtue of being dynamically typed, with no dedicated 'generics' feature needed. Java has a real, compile-time-checked generics system. C has no generics feature at all — void*, macros, and _Generic are all workarounds with meaningfully weaker (or entirely absent) type safety compared to Java's generics.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Writing a genuinely reusable, type-safe container or algorithm is straightforward with Java generics, natural (if unchecked) in Python, and requires real design tradeoffs in C — usually accepting either void* type-unsafety or macro-based textual expansion.

keyPoints: Python's dynamic typing makes most code inherently generic, with no dedicated language feature needed
Java's generics provide genuine compile-time type-parameter checking (with runtime type erasure)
C has no generics — void* pointers, macros, and (in C11+) _Generic are all weaker workarounds
